conversation.content:
Good morning—I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and help you feel supported in these early weeks of motherhood.  

Today we’re going to use a short, well-trusted screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a set of 10 gentle questions that help us understand how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to hear your honest experience so we can figure out the best ways to support you.  

Everything you share stays confidential within our care team, and this space is judgment-free. We’ll go one question at a time, and you can pause or ask for clarification whenever you need. Ready to begin?

First, thinking about the past week:  
Have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

Honestly… most of the time I can still laugh if something’s genuinely funny, but it feels muted—like I have to remind myself to chuckle instead of it just bubbling up the way it used to. I’d say I still find things funny maybe half the time, but it’s not as easy or natural as before I had the baby.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I wouldn’t go that far. I can laugh sometimes, but it feels kind of forced—like I’m working to find the humor rather than it just happening. I’d say it’s only about half the time that I actually feel amused.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to some stuff—like my morning coffee or when my mom brings dinner—but the excitement is kind of dialed down. I’ll think "that’ll be nice," yet it doesn’t give me the same lift it used to. Maybe three-quarters of the time I can muster a little anticipation, but it feels kind of flat compared with before.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. If the baby’s fussy or I can’t get her to nap, I immediately wonder what I’m doing wrong—like I must be missing some cue or not soothing her right. It’s not every second of the day, but probably a few times in the past week I’ve thought, "This is my fault," even when I know logically babies just cry. So, yes, sometimes I do blame myself when things go sideways.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Every now and then I’ll get this sudden knot in my stomach—like, out of nowhere I’ll worry that she’s too quiet or that I missed a feeding cue. It passes pretty quickly once I check on her and she’s fine, so it’s not constant, but it pops up a few times a day without any real trigger.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicked—more like a quick flash of "what if something’s wrong?" than a full-on scared feeling. It’s there and gone in a minute, and I haven’t had any of those breath-catching, heart-racing moments. So, no, I wouldn’t say I’ve been truly scared or panicky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes, yeah. When she won’t settle and the laundry’s piled up, I feel a wave of "I can’t keep up." It’s not all day—mostly I manage—but a couple of times this week it’s felt like everything’s stacking up faster than I can handle it.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, my mood hasn’t messed with my sleep. I’m tired, but once I lie down I drift off pretty easily. Once in a while it takes me an extra few minutes if I’m replaying the day, but I wouldn’t say I’m lying there unhappy and wide-awake.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some stretches of the day—like this little cloud that hangs around even when nothing bad is happening. It’s not constant; maybe a couple of hours here and there, and I can still smile at the baby, but there’s a background “down” feeling that wasn’t there before.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah, that happened twice this week. Once was when she wouldn’t latch and I felt like I was failing her; the other time was after a long night of little catnaps—I just sat on the couch and teared up for a minute. It wasn’t all-day sobbing, just quick bursts that passed after I let it out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, not at all. I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared that, while you can still laugh and anticipate small pleasures, they feel muted and require effort-like humor only bubbling up half the time and excitement feeling "flat." A background "down" cloud lingers for hours most days, and you've caught yourself tearing up twice this week when the baby wouldn't latch or after a long night. Sudden knots of worry appear several times daily even when nothing is wrong, and you sometimes blame yourself when your baby fusses, even though you know babies cry. You're managing basic tasks but occasionally feel swamped, and you're relieved sleep isn't affected and self-harm has never crossed your mind.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 12, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient reports humor feels forced and only occurs about half the time, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly says "Yes... sometimes I do blame myself," matching "Yes, some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, unprovoked worry episodes occurring multiple times daily, matching 'Yes, sometimes</sym>, <sym>Patient describes intermittent overwhelm and feeling that tasks are stacking faster than she can manage, aligning with 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual</sym>, <sym>Patient describes noticeable daily sadness that lingers for hours, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 12 places you in the 12-13 range indicating high possibility of <med>postpartum depression</med>. You endorse five key areas: diminished enjoyment and laughter (Q1=2, Q2=1), frequent unwarranted self-blame (Q3=2), daily unprompted worry (Q4=2), and feeling overwhelmed (Q6=2). These align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>-notably depressed mood most of the day and markedly diminished interest or pleasure. While you deny sleep disruption, panic, or self-harm thoughts, the combination of low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness, and persistent self-blame warrants close follow-up. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or obstetrician within the next week to discuss mood and anxiety symptoms
2. Continue to share these feelings with trusted family or friends; consider resuming any social activities you previously enjoyed
3. Practice brief self-care: short outdoor walks, balanced snacks, and rest when the baby sleeps
4. Keep a simple daily log of mood, worry episodes, and crying spells to review at your follow-up visit
5. Re-screen with EPDS in 2 weeks or sooner if low mood, worry, or overwhelm worsen or if self-harm thoughts emerge
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant < 1 mo  
Date: [today]

Symptoms endorsed (self-report)
- Anhedonia / reduced pleasure: laughs “only ~50% of the time,” anticipatory enjoyment “flat”  
- Depressed mood: “sad cloud” several hours/day  
- Episodic tearfulness: 2 crying spells this week  
- Irrational self-blame: “what am I doing wrong?” when baby fussy  
- Free-floating anxiety: “knot in stomach” several times daily, no trigger  
- Feeling overwhelmed: “wave of ‘I can’t keep up’” 2× this week  

Symptoms denied
- Panic attacks, persistent fear  
- Sleep-onset problems related to mood  
- Thoughts of self-harm

Risk indicators
- Partial anhedonia + low mood + tearfulness → possible minor-mild depressive syndrome  
- Intermittent anxiety without panic → possible comorbid postpartum anxiety  
- No safety concerns (self-harm denied)

Screening impression
Meets sub-threshold criteria for postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms; does not currently meet full diagnostic threshold on brief screen. Continue monitoring, consider standardized tool (EPDS), reassess in 1–2 weeks or sooner if symptoms worsen or safety issues emerge.
